title: End-times sect story
description: Clara Grove criticizes a passing street preacher and then tells a story, learned at school from a girl whose mother had witnessed it, of a sect that calculated the end of the world, gave away everything it owned, and waited on a hillside in white sheets. Nothing happened, and the leaders had to reclaim a milk cow from neighbors so the children would have milk. She links the episode to modern doomsday predictions.

title: Blizzard of 1888; Dakota and Montana blizzards
description: Responding to Isabella Miller's question about the hard winter of 1886-87, Grove recalls the blizzard of 1888 in South Dakota, when her brother barely got the horses home and a neighbor, Mr. Marlett, was kept safely at their house while a schoolteacher froze to death in her schoolhouse for want of a match. She then describes a North Dakota blizzard during which she crawled along a windswept ridge to the barn to water a cow, and heavy snowstorms in Montana.

title: Timber wolf encounter
description: Grove tells of walking home through a pasture after dark as large soft snowflakes fell. She spotted a shadow that proved to be a timber wolf, kept walking slowly, and watched the wolf pass through the settled cattle and horses and head for the hills.

title: Roundhouse work; railroad crews and jobs; Redfield rail service
description: Grove explains her father's work in the railroad roundhouse, turning the turntable by hand and cleaning and polishing engines, and tells how her brother got a fireman's job through the fireman Little Johnny. One interviewer, who also worked as a fireman, remarks that roundhouse work sounds unchanged, and she lists the passenger trains and depots around Redfield, Zell, Rockham, Miranda, and Gettysburg.

title: South Dakota capital fight; Pierre legislators
description: Grove recounts how Redfield, Aberdeen, and Huron contended for the new state capital and how Redfield men hauled away a tiny rival's makeshift capitol building on a wagon by night. The capital went to Pierre, and she tells of the first legislature being snowed in there, legislators staging a mock session with a fake letter from Senator Charlie's wife, and legislators later teaching a citizen penny ante and stripping him of his pennies.

title: Woman's Christian Temperance Union; anti-liquor campaigning
description: Asked about her WCTU work, Grove outlines the organization's international growth under Frances Willard, its broad aims including the eight-hour day and child labor, and her own service as district president and state organizer in Idaho and Washington. She recalls speaking in schools about refusing drinks, an evening in a saloon to use the only phone, confronting a candidate over moderate drinking, and a prank by boys at an infirmary about an ex-WCTU president committed to an asylum.

title: WCTU dues and badges; lilac cane
description: Grove describes the WCTU's dues, white-ribbon, silver and gold badges, and then her sturdy cane cut from a lilac limb, which she used to feel her way through deep snow downtown.

title: Views on nursing homes and old age
description: An interviewer who works at a convalescent home asks Grove about attitudes toward old age. She says living in such a home must be terrible, that she would rather die than go into one, and that people there seem only to wait for death, though some apparently make it home.

title: Closing farewells; plans to meet again
description: Isabella Miller thanks Clara Grove as the interview concludes, and the group exchanges goodbyes and well wishes. They confirm plans to meet again in two weeks, and Clara Grove adds a final comment that she was raised to speak up whenever she has knowledge to contribute.
